report:
## Conclusion

The claim that **increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is not supported by credible scientific evidence**. The available evidence directly examining vaccine exposure—including the number of vaccine antigens received—finds no association with autism.

* A case-control study specifically evaluated children’s cumulative exposure to antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides from vaccines, including exposure on a single day and during the first two years. It found **no evidence of an association with autism**. This is particularly relevant to the “too many vaccines/overloaded immune system” version of the claim.  
https://www.jpeds.com/article/s0022-3476(13)00144-3/fulltext

* A 2014 meta-analysis combined five cohort studies (about 1.3 million children) and five case-control studies (about 10,000 children). It concluded vaccination, MMR, and thimerosal exposure were **not associated** with autism or autism-spectrum disorder.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X14006367

* A Danish nationwide cohort of 657,461 children likewise found MMR vaccination did **not** raise autism risk, including among children with an autistic sibling, a group at higher baseline likelihood of autism.  
https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-2101

**What supports the contrary view?** The best-known source was a 1998 report of only 12 children suggesting a temporal MMR-autism connection. It was a case series—not a study capable of establishing causation—and was later retracted. Subsequent large, controlled studies failed to reproduce its claim.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3136032/

A temporal coincidence can feel persuasive because autism traits are often recognized during the same early-childhood period when many vaccines are given. But timing alone cannot establish causation; the larger controlled evidence does not show that more childhood vaccination causes autism.
